%% assistant This is a canned conversation: nothing here talks to a model or to the network. Each reply is a file read back a few characters at a time through StreamDocument, the way a host would feed it tokens.
Press Enter in the box below (typed text or none) and the next reply plays. The rate slider changes how fast. Things to try while one arrives:
drag across text in any message, then Ctrl+C: one selection for the whole transcript;
scroll up: the pane stops following the end, and takes it up again at the bottom;
the copy button on a code block, and copy as markdown under a message.
The library is at imgui-adv-text and its line breaker is Knuth and Plass's, from Breaking Paragraphs into Lines.
%% user Show me a function, and how you would call it.
%% assistant Here is tokens, which cuts a reply into the pieces this page feeds. The pattern is \s*\S{1,4}|\s+: up to four visible characters with the white space before them.
Joined back together the pieces are the source, which is the only property the replay needs. Call it once per reply, not once per frame: pieces = tokens(text).
%% user Now change it so a piece can be longer.

%% assistant One argument and one changed line. Every existing call keeps working, because most defaults to what was written in the pattern before. Run it with the directory on your path, PATH=$HOME/bin:$PATH (those dollar signs are a shell's and stay text; math is on in this pane, and x^2 is a formula). The diff arrives a line at a time, the block has a toggle for side by side, and this reply ends with it:

+++ b/replay.py
@@ -1,8 +1,9 @@
 import re
 
-def tokens(source: str) -> list[str]:
-    """Pieces of at most four visible characters."""
+def tokens(source: str, most: int = 4) -> list[str]:
+    """Pieces of at most `most` visible characters."""
     # white space travels with the word after it
-    return re.findall(r"\s*\S{1,4}|\s+", source)
+    pattern = r"\s*\S{1,%d}|\s+" % most
+    return re.findall(pattern, source)
 
 assert "".join(tokens("a  bc\n")) == "a  bc\n"
%% user Walk me through adopting this in my own app.
%% assistant Four steps, in the order they stop being optional:
Load the faces once, when the font atlas is built.
A host that already has a font keeps it; these are added beside it.
Build a theme at the pixel height your UI font uses.
Ragged right in one face is what a terminal-like transcript sets. Leave the arguments out for justified Roboto.
A finished message is a BareView and lays out only when the pane's width changes. The message still arriving is a StreamView:

stream = StreamDocument(theme, fontlib_metrics)
view = StreamView(stream, measure)
stream.append(piece)        # as tokens arrive
view.draw(fonts=fonts)      # once a frame
Draw them all into one scrolling child, one after the other.
The views paint no background and claim only their own height, so stacking them is just drawing them.
That is the whole of it. What each step costs:

load faces	once	reading four font files
build theme	once, and on a size change	metrics lookups
finished view	on a width change	one layout of that message
streaming view	each frame something arrived	the unfinished tail only
once, and on a size change
%% user How wide should a line be, and is there a formula for badness?
%% assistant Bringhurst's band is 45 to 75 characters, with 66 the figure usually quoted; this demo's page is 2.25 alphabets, about 65.

Badness is how far a line's glue had to stretch or shrink. The demerits of a line then add the line penalty l and square the sum:

where b is the badness and p the penalty at the break. The breaker minimises \sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i over the whole paragraph, which is what "total fit" means. A price like $5 or $10 is not a formula, and stays text.

A column is not a decoration. It is a decision about how far the eye must travel before it turns around, and almost everything else about a page follows from that one number.

Reading is not a smooth glide along a line of type. The eye moves in jumps, called saccades, and takes in a few characters at each brief stop between them. The jumps along a line are cheap. The expensive one is the return sweep: the long backward flick at the end of a line, which has to land on the first word of the next line and not on the line above it or the line below. Miss that landing and a reader loses a fraction of a second, and something worse than a fraction of a second, which is the sense that the page is on their side. A page that costs them that twice a paragraph is a tiring page however handsome its type.

So a line has a comfortable length, and it is shorter than most people guess. Robert Bringhurst gives sixty-six characters, counting the spaces, as the ideal for a single column of text, and forty-five to seventy-five as the range within which a reader is unlikely to complain. At a normal book size that is something near four inches of line. Set the same text across a ten inch page and every return sweep turns into a small act of navigation, performed forty times a page, by a reader who did not ask to navigate anything.

A page wider than the line it wants is the ordinary case and not the exception. Paper arrives in sheets and screens arrive in windows, and neither was sized by a typographer. The column is the old answer: cut the page into strips each about as wide as a line ought to be, fill the first one, and carry on at the head of the second.
An old answer, and a cheap one

Gutenberg set the forty-two line Bible in two columns, because the manuscripts he was imitating were in two columns, and they were in two columns because a lectern Bible is a large book and a line running the full width of one could not be read standing up. The reason was ergonomic before it was ever aesthetic. It still is.

The newspaper pushed the idea as far as it will go. A broadsheet page is enormous, the material on it is heterogeneous, and none of it is meant to be read in order from the top left corner. Narrow columns solve all three problems at once. They bring the measure back under control; they let an editor move a story without resetting it, because a column of type is a rectangle and rectangles can be shuffled; and they let a reader enter the page anywhere, since a column is short enough to be sampled without commitment.

The price is paid in the spaces. A narrow measure runs nearer thirty characters than sixty, and thirty characters is about five words, which is about four interword spaces. Justify such a line and those four spaces have to absorb the whole of whatever the line was short by. They stretch, visibly, and when two or three consecutive lines stretch in nearly the same places the reader sees a river of white running down the column.
The rivers are not imaginary. They are the eye finding an alignment nobody offered it on purpose.
And no typesetter can talk a reader out of seeing one.

Hyphenation is what makes a narrow justified column possible. It gives the breaker somewhere else to cut, which means the line arrives closer to full, which means the spaces have less work to do. A newspaper without hyphenation is a newspaper set ragged right, and most of them now are. This document is set justified and is not hyphenated, so it is quietly making the argument against itself: watch the interword spacing as you narrow the columns and you will see exactly the effect the paragraph above describes.
The interesting part of a column is not its width. It is its foot.

A vertical list is a sequence of boxes, glue and penalties, in the same way a paragraph is a sequence of boxes, glue and penalties turned on its side. To cut a document into columns is to break that vertical list in the same way the line breaker breaks a horizontal one, and the arithmetic rhymes. Not every position is a legal place to cut. A break may be taken at glue, and only when the thing before that glue is something a reader can see, so that the discarded space falls off the foot of the column rather than reappearing at the head of the next one.

That rule has a consequence here which is worth stating plainly, because it is not obvious and it shaped this page. Between two lines of one paragraph this engine puts interline glue, so a paragraph may be cut between any two of its lines. Between two blocks — two paragraphs, two items of a list, a heading and the text beneath it — it puts a rigid kern instead, and a kern is not a legal breakpoint. So every column break in this document falls inside some paragraph, never between two of them, and any run of short blocks is one indivisible slab however tall it grows. A quoted passage is a single box for the same reason: the bar down its margin has to be exactly as tall as the quote, so the quote is packed whole before anything can ask where it might be cut. Keep the quotations short in a document meant for columns. That is why the one above is.
Three decisions have to be made and none of them is obvious.
Where the cut may fall, which is the question above, and which the document answers rather than the layout engine.

What becomes of the glue that straddles the cut. TeX discards it and then inserts a fresh amount of its own at the top of the fragment, so that the first baseline of every column sits the same distance below the top of the column and the tops line up across the page. The name of that fresh glue is \splittopskip, and a splitter that forgets it produces columns whose first lines are each a little lower or higher than their neighbours, for reasons nobody will be able to see and everybody will be able to feel.

Whether the columns should be balanced. Filling each column to the full height and letting the last one end wherever it ends is honest, cheap, and correct. Balancing, so that the final column of an article is roughly as deep as the others, is what a designer usually wants and what a magazine always wants. It is not free: the usual method is to guess a height, set the whole thing, look at the result, and guess again.

TeX spells the cut \vsplit and it is one of the few primitives with an opinion about the future, since the material it declines to take is handed back for the next column to think about. Balancing is not a primitive at all. In LaTeX it lives in the multicol package, which does exactly the guess, set and guess again described above, and does it well enough that most of its users have never had to find out.

The trade has never agreed on what to call the two commonest faults at a column break, and the disagreement is older than any of us. A single line of a paragraph left stranded at the foot of a column, with the rest of the paragraph moving on to the next one, is bad because it promises a paragraph and does not deliver it. A single line arriving alone at the head of a column, with the rest of its paragraph behind it on the previous one, is worse, because it is a fragment presented as a beginning. One of these is a widow and the other is an orphan; which is which depends entirely on whom you ask, and British printers have long called the second a club line, which at least has the merit of being unambiguous.

The fix for both is the same and it is not a fix at all. It is a penalty — a number attached to a position saying what it would cost to break there — large enough that the breaker will pay for a slightly worse column elsewhere in order to avoid it, and small enough that it will accept the fault rather than fail outright when there is nowhere else to go. That is the whole of the technique, and it is the same technique the line breaker uses, and the same one that keeps a heading from being the last thing on a page.

A heading at the foot of a column is the third fault and the least forgivable, because a heading is a promise about what comes next and there is no next. It is also the easiest to prevent, since a heading and the first lines of the paragraph under it can simply be declared inseparable and moved together.

Every glyph on this page was placed by arithmetic in this repository, including the ones that ended up in the wrong place. The columns were filled by walking the vertical list until the next box would overflow the column height and cutting at the last legal break before it. Nothing was balanced, nothing was hyphenated, and no line was moved by hand to make a screenshot look better.

What a formula does to its line

A formula of plain letters, such as x or a + b = c, is no taller than the words around it, and the lines keep their leading. Scripts hang from the same baseline as the text: the letter in x^2 and in x_i stands where a letter of the sentence would, and x_i^2 carries both at once. A fraction is another matter. The fraction \frac{a}{b} needs more room than a line of words has, so its line is set further from its neighbours, and a fraction of fractions, \frac{\frac{a}{b}}{\frac{c}{d}}, pushes them further again. Only the gaps touching the formula's own line change. The lines above and below this sentence are spaced as they would have been with no formula anywhere in the paragraph, which is what lets a reader's eye keep its place.

A formula is never broken across lines. Drag the measure slider above and watch this one: the sum of an arithmetic progression, a_1 + a_2 + a_3 + \cdots + a_n = \frac{n(a_1 + a_n)}{2}, moves to the next line whole when it no longer fits, and the line it left is stretched to the margin like any other. Parentheses typed as themselves stay the size of the type, as in (\frac{a}{b}). Written with \left and \right they are fitted to what stands between them, as in \left(\frac{a}{b}\right): the font carries eight parentheses of rising height and the smallest that covers the content is the one set; when none does, the largest is used as long as it covers three quarters of it. Dear ImGui draws text very well and will not tell you where it put it. That is a reasonable trade for a debug interface and a poor one for a document, because the moment you want to select a phrase with the mouse you need to know which glyph is under the pointer, and the widget that drew it has already forgotten. Once the layout is ours, hit testing stops being a missing feature and becomes arithmetic over numbers we already computed.

The model is Knuth's. A document is a list of boxes, glue, kerns and penalties. A box has a fixed size, glue has a natural size plus a stretchability and a shrinkability, a kern is rigid space, and a penalty is the cost of breaking a line at that point. The function hpack measures a list and records how far its glue had to stretch; the line breaker then chooses the set of breakpoints with the fewest demerits over the whole paragraph rather than filling each line greedily and hoping.

A greedy filler commits to line one before it has seen line four. Total-fit breaking will loosen an early line by a hair to rescue a later one, and the suite pins that behaviour by enumerating every possible breaking of a short paragraph and checking that the chosen one has the lowest score. See the line breaker for the demerits formula, which is §859 of tex.web transcribed rather than paraphrased.

Badness says how hard one line had to work. Demerits squares it, adds the square of any penalty at the break, and charges extra when two adjacent lines are set very differently — which is why a tight line never sits next to a loose one in well set text.
